Random masking creates a real objective mismatch, but terminal masking is already part of the original BERT4Rec method: its authors explicitly include samples masking only the last item to improve alignment with next-item prediction. Inference appends a reserved [MASK] and scores from that token’s representation. Thus, increasing terminal-task exposure is a grounded experiment, although improved HR@10 under this benchmark remains unproven. [Original BERT4Rec, §3.6](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690).

Recency-based Sampling of Sequences (RecSys 2022) argues that arbitrary masked-item reconstruction is only weakly aligned with recommendation and samples recent targets more frequently while retaining nonzero probability for older targets. Its experiments concern other backbones, so adapting this sampling to BERT4Rec is a hypothesis, not an established BERT4Rec result. More recently, Masked History Learning (2025 preprint; revised 2026) transitions from history reconstruction toward inference-aligned next-item training, but studies generative recommendation rather than a direct BERT4Rec masking comparison. [Recency sampling](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643), [MHL](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.23649).

Practical single-model experiment: mix random Cloze batches with terminal-mask batches generated from training-only prefixes; optionally increase the terminal fraction late in training. Sample prefix endpoints with a tunable recency bias. For each terminal example, replace its target with [MASK] and exclude every later interaction, preserving bidirectional attention over the visible prefix. Multi-token suffix masking is a separate hypothesis because it changes the prediction horizon. With left padding, read the appended mask at the final nonpadding index—normally L−1—never count(nonpadding)−1. Keep training, checkpoint loading, and predictor construction identical.
